Disappearing texts in Brussels spark an accountability crisis as top EU officials wipe records.
Burn after reading
Evidence: Institutional cybersecurity, Disappearing executive records, Democratic transparency
#EU #Transparency 🌐

The European Commission claims deleting executive text messages and using disappearing chats is a necessary cybersecurity policy that protects official communications from operational compromise.
Stated Judgement: (+0.87, +0.82) — Greater Good

By systematically erasing high-level texts with heads of state and pharma CEOs, the Commission creates accountability-free zones that actively subvert EU public access and FOI regulations.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.70, -0.77) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction. The Commission’s systematic purging of official communications collapses public trust and institutional oversight.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 14.8, z: 3)

- EU Commission: FAIL (-0.78, -0.82) — Deletes executive texts to block scrutiny.
- EU Ombudsman: PASS (+0.80, +0.65) — Enforces document retention and oversight.
- Politico Coverage: PASS (+0.65, +0.45) — Accurately reports institutional clash.
European Ombudsman Teresa Anjinho accused the Commission of feet-dragging after it confirmed it will keep deleting Ursula von der Leyen's texts, including diplomacy with French President Macron.

The Bright Side:
The European Ombudsman and EU courts are actively pushing back against executive opacity, demanding that digital governance adapt to maintain public records.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The failure occurs on the Metaphysical Plane (WHO). The Commission presents auto-deletion as protecting the institution, when in reality it shields individual officials from legal accountability.

Social Physics Analysis:
Commission leadership executes a Smart Selfish Maneuver: shielding secret executive deal-making behind the manufactured pretext of cybersecurity. Instead of building transparent systems, they hoard power by destroying the digital paper trail.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. Treating public records as disposable destroys democratic legitimacy.

The Unavoidable Truth: If public policy is decided via text, those texts are public documents.
The Unavoidable Lie: Erasing official negotiation records is a cybersecurity necessity rather than an evasion of oversight.

Alethekanon:
Governance via disappearing messages is an architectural subversion of democracy. When an institution designs its search protocols to only find what it registered, transparency becomes a farce.

Awwthekanon:
Citizens deserve to trust that their leaders aren't hiding major public decisions behind locked screens and disappearing chats. True integrity means having the courage to keep the lights on.

Brothekanon:
Bruh, calling 'I deleted my texts with Pfizer' a cybersecurity feature is peak bureaucratic comedy. If regular folks tried that with tax receipts, they'd get audited yesterday.

Spirithekanon:
"For everyone practicing evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his deeds should be exposed." John 3:20 FAIL
Wiping official records to evade accountability directly violates the fundamental duty of transparency.

A weekly newsletter on campaigning, lobbying and political influence in the EU.

By MARI ECCLES

Tips, tales, traumas to [email protected] | View in your browser

Hello and welcome to EU Influence! I’m Mari Eccles. Regular readers will know how much time I spend on LinkedIn tracking job moves, deciphering subtweets and, on the most thrilling of days, following incredibly petty below-the-line spats between lobbyists I barely know (please send me your favorites).

But this week I briefly mistook LinkedIn for property site Immoweb after stumbling across this post by Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen’s cabinet member Xavier Coget, who is selling his villa in Uccle. It costs €1.6 million, in case you’re interested.

In non-real estate news:

— EU officials’ use of disappearing messages risks creating “accountability-free zones,” the bloc’s watchdog warns.

— Oslo’s current EU influence strategy isn’t working.

— MCC Brussels announces its successor (just don’t call it MCC 2.0).

NOTHING TO SEE HERE: The EU is increasingly keeping the public in the dark, the bloc’s watchdog has warned — in part because top dogs in Brussels delete their texts. European Ombudsman Teresa Anjinho said text messages, disappearing chats and decisions shaped by artificial intelligence make it harder than ever to scrutinize the EU institutions, and she accused officials of feet-dragging and evasion when it comes to responding to requests for documents.

Time for a rewrite: Anjinho said the bloc’s ancient access-to-documents rules are failing citizens and need updating. “Twenty-five years ago, the regulation was designed for a world of paper trails, physical archives, and analog processes,” she said in a speech on Wednesday. Now, negotiations happen via texts, “where governance increasingly relies on data flows that leave no traditional paper trail behind, and where decisions can even be made by algorithms.”

Funny you mention that: Just last week, the Commission confirmed that it will continue to delete President Ursula von der Leyen‘s texts — even though the ombudsman said doing so amounted to maladministration. Earlier this year, Anjinho’s office told von der Leyen and EU commissioners to retain messages exchanged with heads of state and government after a complaint from outlet Follow the Money, which (unsuccessfully) sought access to texts between the Commission chief and French President Emmanuel Macron. In a private message to von der Leyen in 2024, exclusively reported by POLITICO, Macron attempted to blow up the EU-Mercosur trade deal.

But but but: Von der Leyen’s team on Friday wrote to the ombudsman to say that keeping hold of messages for as long as it might take to challenge a Freedom of Information request refusal — up to two years — “cannot be reconciled with the necessary cybersecurity measures.”

War of words: In her speech this week, Anjinho hit back. “An institution cannot let a security architecture quietly decide what is a document in the first place,” she said, adding: “If the content is relevant to an EU policy and activity, or the decision-making process, it should survive long enough to be assessed, whatever channel it travelled through.”

That stings: The problem can be neatly summed up with the way the Commission searched for von der Leyen’s texts with Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla during Covid vaccine negotiations. “The search that followed looked only for what had already been registered — which is to say, it was designed not to find what it was asked to find,” Anjinho said. The EU’s General Court later ruled that EU institutions cannot hollow out access rights by failing to register messages.
